claims.text: Generative AI and assessments | Students - UCL

evidence.quote:
For Category 1, you might use GenAI tools to help you revise and prepare, but the work you complete for the assessment should be your own.
In Category 2, you could use GenAI to get ideas, help draft your work, or even proofread what you've written. Just make sure you keep a note of how you've used GenAI, so that you can acknowledge it afterwards. You won't lose marks just for having used GenAI.
Category 3 is a lot like category 2, but there will also be some essential use of GenAI as part of the assessment.

evidence.quote: It's okay to use GenAI to help with spelling and grammar, and even with the tone of your language. However, make sure it isn't changing the content and meaning of what you've written. You should always understand the work you submit.

claims.text: CLIE Policy on Student Use of Generative AI 2026–27

evidence.quote: CLIE’s policy is based on UCL’s three categories of GenAI use in assessment. topics.title: Disclosure
topics.summary: Acknowledgement is required whenever GenAI has been used as a functional tool to assist in creating academic work (drafting, planning, structuring). Minimum acknowledgement requires tool name/version, publisher, URL, and single-sentence context. Where required by standard referencing styles (APA, Chicago) or departmental guidelines, the GenAI tool may be cited as an author in addition to functional acknowledgement.
topics.scope: Assessment/teaching/doctoral/publisher/data service as identified by the bound evidence.
actions: Include tool name, version, publisher, URL, and single-sentence usage statement in coursework
Check departmental briefs for any required appendix of prompts or tracked changes
Follow standard referencing styles (e.g. APA, Chicago) if citation in reference list is required

claims.text: Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills

evidence.quote:
The use of GenAI must be acknowledged in any piece of academic work where it has been used as a functional tool to assist in the process of
creating
the academic work, such as drafting ideas and planning or structuring written materials.
evidence.title: Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills
Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills

evidence.quote:
Minimum requirement to include in acknowledgement:
Name and version of the GenAI system used; e.g. Microsoft Copilot (version GPT-4); ChatGPT-3.5
Publisher (company that made the |GenAI system); e.g. Microsoft; OpenAI
URL of the GenAI system.
Brief description (single sentence) of context in which the tool was used.
For example:
I acknowledge the use of Microsoft Copilot (version GPT-4, Microsoft, https://m365.cloud.microsoft/chat) to summarise my initial notes and to proofread my final draft.
evidence.title: Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills

evidence.quote:
Further requirements may be stipulated by a department, academic programme or individual teaching staff, or for a particular assignment, and must be made clear to students when an assignment is set. Additional requirements may include expanded description in an ‘Appendix’ or ‘Methods’ section, such as:
If relevant, the prompt(s) used to generate a response in the GenAI system.
The date the output was generated.
The output obtained (e.g. a ‘link to chat’ if ChatGPT, or a compilation of all output generated as an appendix).
How the output was changed for use or incorporation into a piece of work (e.g. a tracked-changes document or a descriptive paragraph).
evidence.title: Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills

evidence.quote:
A GenAI tool cannot be classed as an author – it cannot take responsibility for its work, nor does it generate original ideas but reproduces ideas found elsewhere.
A primary function of a reference list is so the reader can refer to the original source, which is not possible with AI generated content.
This proposal therefore favours the approach of most academic publishers (1-3), which stipulates GenAI systems should not be cited as an author nor included as a source in the reference list.
evidence.title: Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills

evidence.quote: Where a student or researcher is required to use a standard referencing style which has specific rules for citing and referencing GenAI, the rules of the citation style should be followed, in addition to acknowledging the use of GenAI as outlined above. This may require the use of in-text citations and reference list entries where the GenAI tool is listed as an author. E.g. APA, Chicago.
evidence.title: Acknowledging and referencing GenAI - References, citations and avoiding plagiarism - Library Skills

evidence.quote: We therefore do not allow AI or LLM tools to be listed as an author on any research-based work published by UCL Press.
evidence.title: UCL Press Journals Editorial Policies

evidence.quote: Broadly, the use of AI-assisted technologies in the creation, editing, manipulating, enhancing, adjusting, obscuring, moving, removing or introducing any new specific feature within an image or figure, is not accepted.
evidence.title: UCL Press Journals Editorial Policies

evidence.quote: It would, however, be acceptable for AI-assisted technologies and tools that are used as part of research design or methodology (such as in AI-assisted imaging approaches to generate or interpret the underlying research data, for example in data visualisation), but this must be clearly declared as part of the methodology and full disclosure about what tools were used, how the tools were used, when this was used and explicably outline which images or figures were created using these tools. Where necessary, authors may be asked to provide pre-AI-adjusted versions of images and/or the composite raw images used to create the final submitted versions, for editorial assessment.
evidence.title: UCL Press Journals Editorial Policies

evidence.quote: Editors and peer reviewers must treat a manuscript that is under review confidentially and must not submit the manuscript through an AI-assisted technology or tool. Submitting any manuscript or data the manuscript reports on through any AI-assisted technology or tool may incur a breach in confidentiality, proprietary rights and data, including personally identifiable information.
evidence.title: UCL Press Journals Editorial Policies
